target.title: fix(group): keep group id display truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #109993

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `shortenGroupId` in `src/config/sessions/group.ts` uses `String.prototype.slice()` which operates on UTF-16 code units. When a surrogate pair (e.g. emoji like 🚀 🎉) straddles the truncation boundary, `.slice()` produces orphan surrogates that render as garbled text in the UI.

**Root Cause**: `trimmed.slice(0, 6)` and `trimmed.slice(-4)` can cut through the middle of a surrogate pair. For example, when a high surrogate lands at code-unit position 5 (the last position of the prefix), `slice(0, 6)` returns the high surrogate without its matching low surrogate. Same issue for the suffix.

**Solution**: Replace `.slice(0, 6)` with `truncateUtf16Safe(trimmed, 6)` and `.slice(-4)` with `sliceUtf16Safe(trimmed, -4)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`. These helpers detect surrogate pair boundaries and adjust the cut position to keep pairs whole. Also exported `shortenGroupId` for direct testing.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-35-generic / Node.js v25.9.0 / tsx v4.22.4

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
npx tsx scripts/evidence-shortenGroupId.mts
```

The script directly imports `shortenGroupId` from `src/config/sessions/group.ts` and compares its output against the old `String.prototype.slice` implementation across 10 test cases covering ASCII, CJK, emoji, and mixed scripts.

**After-fix evidence**:
```
HEAD: e7f7d015201312c256211c54616d9bcde0954fe9

==================================================================================================================================
  shortenGroupId -- OLD (String.prototype.slice) vs NEW (UTF-16 safe)
==================================================================================================================================

 #  Test case                       OLD result                  NEW result                  Status
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1  ASCII, <=14 chars -- no trunc    C0123456789abc              C0123456789abc              OK
  2  ASCII, >14 chars                C01234...abcd               C01234...abcd               OK
  3  slice(0,6) hits pair mid        abcde\uD83C...lmno          abcde...lmno                <<< OLD HAS ORPHAN SURROGATE
  4  slice(-4) hits pair mid         abcdef...\uDF89mno          abcdef...mno                <<< OLD HAS ORPHAN SURROGATE
  5  both ends hit pairs             abcde\uD83C...\uDF89mno     abcde...mno                 <<< OLD HAS ORPHAN SURROGATE
  6  CJK channel name                项目-Alp...道讨论群               项目-Alp...道讨论群               OK
  7  emoji-rich group                abcde\uD83D...nopq          abcde...nopq                <<< OLD HAS ORPHAN SURROGATE
  8  slack-like channel id           slack:...EFGH               slack:...EFGH               OK
  9  pair at slice(0,6) edge         abcde\uD83C...pqrs          abcde...pqrs                <<< OLD HAS ORPHAN SURROGATE
 10  pair at slice(-4) edge          abcdef...\uDF89opq          abcdef...opq                <<< OLD HAS ORPHAN SURROGATE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary: 6 cases had orphan surrogates in OLD path. 4 cases pass (NEW has 0 orphans).
All NEW results are UTF-16 safe -- no broken surrogate pairs.
```

**Observed result after the fix**: The new `shortenGroupId` produces valid UTF-16 output in all 10 test cases. 6 out of 10 cases produced orphan surrogates (shown as `\uD83C`, `\uD83D`, `\uDF89`) under the old `.slice()` implementation -- the fix eliminates all of them.

**What was not tested**: Full Gateway runtime with real session-group display data. The change is scoped to one pure function and does not affect networking, external services, or any runtime behavior beyond the string truncation path.

## Tests and validation

The existing `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` unit tests already cover the surrogate-safe helpers.
The evidence script (`scripts/evidence-shortenGroupId.mts`) validates the `shortenGroupId` end-to-end integration against both old and new implementations.

- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(process): Windows exec/read empty output when detached spawn leaks
target.body:
Closes #105528

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Windows users running OpenClaw under a headless host (Scheduled Task / service) can see `exec` and `read` tools return empty output with no error when `detached: true` reaches Node `child_process.spawn`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Call sites already try to disable detached spawn on Windows, but those guards are scattered. Fixes an issue where Windows users with SQLite-backed sessions could hit repeated `EPERM` errors during transcript archival, causing maintenance to retry the same stale sessions and repeatedly stall the gateway.

target.title: fix(ci): script-only changes cold-start every Node job
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary package-script edits invalidated the protected pnpm dependency snapshot, forcing every Linux Node CI job to reinstall an unchanged dependency graph. During the July 17 rollout, one root test-script addition rotated the fingerprint; dozens of read-only shard jobs then rebuilt disposable trees instead of restoring the warm snapshot.

## Why This Change Was Made

The dependency fingerprint now canonicalizes every tracked workspace manifest. Under the exact audited root install-hook contract it hashes dependency fields, pnpm install lifecycle entries, lockfile/package-manager inputs, and the source files those hooks execute, while ignoring formatting and ordinary test/build scripts that `pnpm install` never runs.

Unknown lifecycle hooks fail closed until their source inputs are added to the contract. This avoids both false cache misses and unsafe reuse of stale lifecycle output. Dependency, lockfile, package-manager, runtime, platform, audited hook-source, and frozen-mode changes still invalidate normally.

Read-only PR jobs with a stale protected snapshot detach the sticky bind and install into runner-local storage. Sticky cold installs disable pnpm's internal fetch retries and make up to three bounded full-install attempts from the progressively warmed store. A timeout always remains a failure; no log output can convert a partial install into success. Non-sticky installs retain two attempts.

## User Impact

CI keeps the warm dependency snapshot after ordinary script-only changes. Real dependency/install changes rebuild safely. Cold transitions tolerate transient registry failures without minute-long nested retry backoffs.

No product runtime behavior changes.

## Evidence

- Main run [29607109226](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29607109226) reproduced the original script-only fingerprint rotation.
- Cold-transition run [29610614176](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29610614176) proved the v2 fingerprint path: the old marker differed, the first install populated the tree, and the retry completed in 290 ms.
- Follow-up run [29612450308](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29612450308) exposed the remaining network edge: pnpm printed `Done in 1m 14.9s`, then optional platform-tarball retries retained the process until the second four-minute timeout. The current head removes those inner fetch retries, retries the complete frozen transaction up to three times, and never trusts a completion banner.
- Exact-head run [29616260423](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29616260423) validates the final branch and is being monitored through merge.
- Workflow guard: 81 passed, 1 skipped. Workflow actionlint, zizmor, and interpolation checks passed.
- Fingerprint regression coverage proves ordinary script/format changes stay warm; dependency, lockfile, audited hook-source, optional-file presence, and frozen-mode changes invalidate; unaudited root or workspace lifecycle hooks fail closed.
- Canvas watcher, gateway approval, and install-policy timeout flakes passed five bounded repetitions after fixes (18 + 173 + 22 tests per iteration). Canvas now tests the canonical watcher root; async assertions allow loaded CI scheduling without changing production timeouts.
- Focused routing/package suite: 377 passed, 1 skipped before the final fail-closed edit; the affected workflow guard reran green afterward.
- Final branch Autoreview passed at 0.93 with no accepted/actionable findings. Earlier accepted findings drove whole-process timeout ownership, removal of banner-based false success, and fail-closed lifecycle handling.
- Targeted formatting, docs MDX, workflow validation, and `git diff --check` passed.

## Rollout

The protected dependency disk has one non-PR writer. PR jobs consume read-only clones and cannot publish the new v2 marker. After merge, the cache warmer will publish v2; the next PR/main consumer must log `Sticky dependency snapshot matches the install fingerprint; skipping pnpm install`. Post-merge monitoring will confirm restore/save evidence, setup timings, and absence of sticky-disk or cache-race errors.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): cancel unread response body in crabline injection
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #109992

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the `postCrablineInbound()` error path. When a Crabline inbound injection returns a non-ok HTTP status, the response body ReadableStream is now explicitly cancelled before throwing the error, preventing an unread stream resource leak.

**What NOT changed**: No change to the happy path — successful responses still pass through to the complete handler as before. No change to the Crabline injection logic, request construction, or error message format. No new dependencies added.

**Why NOT changed**: The body cancel is only needed before throwing, since the stream becomes unreachable after the throw. On success the body is not consumed by this function — the entire response is forwarded — so no cancel is required on the ok path.

**merge-risk**: Minimal — the pattern `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is a standard no-op on success and a no-throw guard on failure. It affects only the single error path in `crabline-transport.ts`. Zero risk of regression on the ok path.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When a Crabline inbound injection HTTP request returns a non-ok response (e.g., 502, 400), the response body stream is left unread, causing a potential resource leak (unconsumed ReadableStream). Node.js will emit a warning for unconsumed response bodies in future versions.

**Root Cause**: `postCrablineInbound()` throws immediately in the `if (!response.ok)` branch without cancelling the unread response body, leaving the stream open for garbage collection to clean up — which is non-deterministic and can retain buffers until GC runs.

**Solution**: Add `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the error path to eagerly release the stream. The `cancel()` method (Fetch API standard) releases the stream's resources. The `?.` optional chaining guards against a null body (e.g., 204 No Content responses or server errors that omit a body). The `.catch()` ensures that a double-cancel or rejection from the stream implementation does not propagate.

## Evidence

### Mocked body cancel behavior (covers the code contract)

The following edge cases were verified with a TypeScript demo exercising the exact same `body.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` pattern:

```
--- Body cancel before throw ---
Body cancelled before throw: YES ✅
Error: Crabline injection failed (502)

--- Cancel rejection handled ---
Cancel rejection suppressed: ✅
Error: Crabline injection failed (400)

--- Null body safe ---
Null body cancel: safe ✅

--- Double cancel safe ---
Double cancel: safe ✅ (n=2)

COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0
```

### Crabline transport unit tests (17/17 pass)

All existing crabline transport tests pass with the fix applied, confirming no regression on the success path:

```

 ✓ crabline transport > injects Telegram native commands through the shared transport adapter 37ms
 ✓ crabline transport > observes Telegram preview edits through the shared transport adapter 41ms
 ✓ crabline transport > configures OpenClaw's Slack plugin against a Crabline local provider server 15ms
 ✓ crabline transport > injects inbound messages through Crabline and mirrors Slack sends ... 36ms
 ✓ crabline transport > configures OpenClaw's WhatsApp plugin against a Crabline Baileys ... 4ms
 ✓ crabline transport > injects WhatsApp inbound messages through Crabline into normalized state 26ms
 ✓ crabline transport > binds Signal config and normalizes transport targets 29ms
 ✓ crabline transport > normalizes native Signal JSON-RPC sends into outbound state 27ms
 ✓ crabline transport > binds Mattermost config and normalizes transport targets 41ms
 ✓ crabline transport > normalizes native Mattermost post creation into outbound state 39ms
 ✓ crabline transport > binds Matrix config and normalizes transport targets 69ms
 ✓ crabline transport > normalizes native Matrix room message sends into outbound state 47ms
 ✓ crabline transport > configures Zalo and normalizes native message sends 42ms
 ✓ crabline transport > injects inbound messages through Crabline and mirrors Telegram ... 62ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  17 passed (17)
```

### Real QA Lab runtime evidence

The actual failure scenario (a Crabline inbound injection returning HTTP 502/400 in a QA Lab run) requires:
- A running QA Lab instance with a Crabline adapter configured against a live provider
- A provider or network condition that causes the admin inbound injection to return a non-2xx status

This is not reproducible in a local dev environment without the full QA Lab runtime infrastructure. The mock-based demo above verifies the exact code contract (`response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` semantics), and the existing unit tests confirm no regression on the success path.

## Tests and validation

target.title: fix: gateway startup fails on legacy default channel allowlists
target.body:
Fixes #108421
Related to #108299

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users upgrading from OpenClaw `2026.7.1` to
`2026.7.2-beta.1` could no longer start the Gateway when a legacy
`credentials/whatsapp-default-allowFrom.json` file remained and no
`channels.whatsapp` section existed.

The startup migration reported the legacy file as unresolved and left it in
place. `openclaw doctor --fix` detected the same warning but could not complete
the migration, so Gateway startup continued to refuse readiness.

## Why This Change Was Made

Legacy scoped allowFrom filenames are parsed as a channel ID plus an account
key. The migration already knows `whatsapp` is a bundled channel through
`CHANNEL_IDS`, but it previously accepted the `default` account suffix only
when that account had also been discovered from channel configuration or
bindings. With no `channels.whatsapp` section, the explicit `default` suffix
therefore had no configured match and was classified as unresolved.

The parser now recognizes an explicit `default` suffix as the canonical default
account when, and only when, the parsed channel is a bundled OpenClaw channel.
The existing migration then imports the allowlist into the shared SQLite pairing
state and removes the legacy JSON file.

This is intentionally narrower than adding `default` to every discovered
channel:

- External plugin channels still require an explicit configured account match.
- Sanitized account-name collisions remain ambiguous.
- Filenames with overlapping channel/account interpretations remain ambiguous.
- No Doctor orchestration, startup readiness, configuration, SQLite schema, or
  plugin migration behavior changes.

Special-casing WhatsApp was also considered, but rejected because `default` is
the canonical account ID across bundled channels. Restricting the general rule
to `CHANNEL_IDS` preserves the core/plugin ownership boundary without adding a
channel-specific exception.

## User Impact

Affected upgrades can automatically migrate
`whatsapp-default-allowFrom.json` into the SQLite pairing state under the
`default` account. The legacy file is removed after a successful import, so
startup migrations complete without requiring users to recreate channel
configuration or manually relocate the file.

## Evidence

The positive regression test creates the reported version-1 object shape with:

- bundled channel `whatsapp`;
- no `channels.whatsapp` configuration;
- an explicit `default` account suffix;
- properly formatted fictional E.164 allowlist entries.

It verifies that:

- no unresolved warning is emitted;
- all entries are stored in SQLite under `whatsapp/default`;
- the migration reports success; and
- the legacy source file is removed.

A negative regression test creates
`custom-channel-default-allowFrom.json` for an external configured channel with
no configured account. It verifies that the migration remains unresolved,
leaves the source file in place, and writes no SQLite allowlist.

Executed locally:

  — 6 tests passed;

- `pnpm format` for both changed files; and
- `git diff --check`.

Blacksmith Testbox tooling is unavailable on this host.

target.title: fix(ui): neutralize spreadsheet formulas in usage CSV export
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI usage page lets operators download session and daily cost data as CSV (`ui/src/pages/usage/view.ts` export menu → `buildSessionsCsv` / `buildDailyCsv` in `ui/src/pages/usage/query.ts`). Two cell-safety corners in `csvEscape` were missing:

1. **Spreadsheet formula injection.** `session.label` is user/agent-controlled (stored via the gateway session store, `src/gateway/server-methods/usage.ts`), and `agentId` / `channel` / `model` flow through the same row builder. A label whose first non-whitespace character is `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` (or their full-width forms) is executed as a formula when the exported CSV is opened in Excel/LibreOffice/Numbers — the classic CSV injection vector (e.g. a label of `=HYPERLINK(...)`).
2. **Bare carriage return breaks rows.** The quote trigger `[",\n]` did not include `\r`, so a label containing a lone `\r` was emitted unquoted and split the row in strict CSV parsers.

## Why This Change Was Made

`csvEscape` now runs every cell through `neutralizeSpreadsheetFormulaCell` (prepend a leading `'` only when the cell's first non-whitespace character is a formula prefix) and the quote trigger covers `\r` as well. This mirrors the merged google-meet attendance CSV fix https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109725 (formula neutralization) and its follow-up https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109926 (`\r` quoting), keeping one canonical cell-safety pattern across the repo — with the neutralization predicate narrowed per review so plain whitespace-prefixed text keeps its bytes. The same fix for this site was previously proposed in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/44376, which was auto-closed by the contributor queue cap (`too-many-prs`), not rejected on merit.

No behavior changes for ordinary cells: values without a formula prefix render byte-identical to before (only `\r` now adds CSV quotes, like `\n` already did). Regression coverage locks neutralization for ASCII and full-width prefixes, whitespace-prefixed formulas, byte preservation of tab/space/CR-prefixed plain labels, and bare `\r` quoting.

Fix classification: additive hardening of an existing export path; no config, API, or SDK surface changes.

## User Impact

- Exported usage CSVs can no longer smuggle executable spreadsheet formulas through session labels or ids.
- Labels containing carriage returns no longer corrupt row boundaries when the CSV is re-imported.
- Plain labels that happen to start with a tab, space, or CR keep their exact bytes in the export (no stray apostrophe).

Follow-up to #96230.

## What Problem This Solves

The restart-recovery fix landed with duplicated mutation wrappers, repeated state-machine branches, and repeated test assertions that made an already delicate correctness surface harder to audit.

## Why This Change Was Made

Compress the implementation without changing recovery behavior: co-locate private Plugin SDK mutations with their public runtime owner, share identical reservation validation, reuse the canonical recovery-candidate predicate, and remove dead/redundant parameters and branches. Keep storage, lifecycle, dispatch, failure, and orchestration modules separate because each owns a distinct durability or dependency boundary.

Production surface: 5,479 -> 5,349 lines (-130). Focused test surface: 8,874 -> 8,852 lines (-22). Every existing recovery scenario test remains; only repeated SDK assertions were factored.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(daemon): retry launchd reload bootstrap instead of kickstart
target.body:
Closes #110137.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users restarting the gateway in reload mode on macOS launchd would end up with the service unloaded and stranded. After bootout, the handoff fell back to kickstart -k, which cannot restore a label that is already unloaded, so the gateway never came back.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reload handoff now retries launchctl bootstrap with launchctl print verification after the bootout wait loop, and no longer uses kickstart as reload recovery. Kickstart remains the path for kickstart mode only.

## User Impact

macOS launchd reloads that change plist content should bring the gateway back instead of leaving it unloaded after a bootstrap race (EIO / Bootstrap failed: 5).

## AI assistance

Assisted by Cursor/Grok. Human: Stan Shih (stantheman0128).

## Evidence

```text
pnpm exec vitest run src/daemon/launchd-restart-handoff.test.ts
# reload assertion test: PASS (retries bootstrap and verifies launchctl print after reload bootout)
# 3 passed including reload + start-after-exit + invalid label
# 2 failed on Windows only: kickstart/sanitize tests expect /Users/test/... log paths;
# received Windows TEMP paths. Same class of Windows path expectation on this host;
# A/B not blamed on this diff (reload script content assertions pass).
```

Script assertions now require bootstrap_retry_count= and forbid launchctl kickstart -k in reload mode.

Related: #109755

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes three meeting-browser recovery edge cases deferred from the meeting-bot extraction: transcript polling could replay retained lines under shifted indices after a page retention gap, untargeted tab recovery could choose a provider sign-in tab before an active meeting, and talk-back could report ready before the microphone state was known.

The transcript store now retains one contiguous tail and preserves its cross-epoch offset whenever the page cursor jumps. Untargeted recovery ranks normalized meeting URLs before login fallbacks. Talk-back now treats an unknown microphone state as transiently browser-unverified and requires an explicit unmuted state; the policy is documented inline and reuses the existing retry reason.

Unknown remains blocked until the browser reports `micMuted: false`; the live two-party proof is explicitly waived because the exact branches are covered by deterministic browser-proxy and runtime regressions, while full observation requires a private participant, controllable microphone, and cursor/readiness telemetry.

target.title: fix(feishu): lock timeoutMs preflight abort for stalled DNS lookup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Feishu app registration can hang when SSRF DNS/proxy preflight never completes. Without an entry-point regression on `beginAppRegistration`, a future change can stop forwarding `timeoutMs` into `fetchWithSsrFGuard` and leave onboarding stuck before HTTP dispatch.

## Why This Change Was Made

Current `main` (after [#105549](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/105549)) owns registration deadlines via **guard top-level `timeoutMs`**, not `AbortSignal.timeout()` in `RequestInit`. `beginAppRegistration(domain, options?)` still accepts test-only `fetchImpl` / `lookupFn` / `timeoutMs`.

This PR is test-only: it locks that contract for a never-resolving `lookupFn`, asserting `TimeoutError` + `message: "request timed out"` and that `fetchImpl` is never called. Shared SSRF suites already cover stalled DNS; this asserts the Feishu entry point still forwards `timeoutMs` into that owner.

**Note for review:** Rewriting this regression to `AbortSignal.timeout()` would regress #105549 and does not match current `main` (`extensions/feishu/src/app-registration.ts` still forwards `timeoutMs` into `fetchWithSsrFGuard`).

## User Impact

No runtime change. Contributors get a Feishu-local regression that fails if registration stops honoring the guard-owned preflight deadline.

## Evidence

| Layer | Proof |
| --- | --- |
| Head | `fc27e5dacd53197e5ac8a770a2bceed491ff5d65` (1 commit on latest `main` `282879b…`) |
| Scope | 1 file test-only (`app-registration.test.ts`) |
| Contract on main | `beginAppRegistration` options still include `lookupFn` / `timeoutMs` / `fetchImpl` |
| L1 | focused vitest: stall DNS + hang headers |

```text
pnpm exec vitest run extensions/feishu/src/app-registration.test.ts -t "preflight lookup stalls|never return headers"
→ 2 passed

[feishu preflight stall proof] timed_out=true name=TimeoutError message=request timed out elapsed_ms=81 fetch_called=0
[feishu fetchFeishuJson hang proof] timed_out=true name=TimeoutError elapsed_ms=100
```

Sibling on main already covers post-connect hang (`times out registration POSTs when accounts never return headers`). This PR adds the **preflight/DNS stall before fetch** path (`fetch_called=0`).

target.title: Runtime context carrier positioned AFTER user message causes severe model confusion and reasoning token waste
target.body:
## Problem

OpenClaw injects a runtime context carrier (~15K chars of session metadata, conversation history, tool descriptions) as a `role: "user"` message. By default, `relocateCurrentRuntimeContextCarrierToTail()` moves this carrier to **AFTER** the user's actual message:

```
[role: user] "actual user text"                    ← real user message
[role: user] "OpenClaw runtime context for the..."  ← carrier injected AFTER
[role: assistant] response
```

This causes **severe model confusion**. The model sees two consecutive `role: user` messages and cannot determine whether the second one is:
- A new instruction from the user
- A duplicate delivery of the first message
- System metadata to ignore
- A follow-up request

## Impact

### Reasoning token waste

Models waste thousands of reasoning tokens per turn trying to disambiguate the carrier from a real user message. In one observed case (GLM-5.2 with thinking enabled), the model produced **100+ lines of circular reasoning** over 2+ minutes before responding — repeatedly questioning whether the carrier was a new message, a duplicate, or metadata, going back and forth without resolution.

This reasoning overhead is particularly costly because:
1. It happens on **every turn** (the carrier is injected on every API call)
2. It occurs on **every API call within a turn** (tool-call roundtrips re-send the carrier)
3. Reasoning tokens may exceed Telegram message limits, causing delivery failures
4. Cross-turn reasoning is dropped by design, so the model re-derives the same confusion each turn

### Cache optimization trade-off is negligible

The `relocateCurrentRuntimeContextCarrierToTail()` function's stated purpose is prompt-cache optimization: carrier at tail means only the trailing carrier re-bills per turn; carrier before the user message means the whole tail re-bills.

The cache savings are ~50-200 tokens/turn (one user message worth). The reasoning penalty from model confusion is thousands of tokens. This is not a worthwhile trade-off.

## Root Cause

### Code path

In `selection-*.js` (call site of `convertToLlm`):

```javascript
activeSession.agent.convertToLlm = async (messages) =>
  await baseConvertToLlm(
    relocateCurrentRuntimeContextCarrierToTail(   // ← MOVES carrier to tail
      normalizeMessagesForLlmBoundary(messages, buildBoundaryOptions())
    )
  );
```

The underlying `stripHistoricalRuntimeContextCustomMessages()` already positions carriers **IMMEDIATELY BEFORE** the active user message — which is the semantically correct position. `relocateCurrentRuntimeContextCarrierToTail()` then overrides this by moving them to the absolute tail.

### Carrier header wording

The carrier header reads: `"OpenClaw runtime context for the immediately preceding user message."` — this is only semantically correct when the carrier follows the user message. If the carrier precedes the user message, the wording should reflect that.

## Proposed Fix

1. **Remove or make configurable** the `relocateCurrentRuntimeContextCarrierToTail()` call. The default position (before the user message, as set by `stripHistoricalRuntimeContextCustomMessages()`) is correct.

2. **Update the header wording** to be position-agnostic or reflect the new default position.

3. Consider whether two consecutive `role: user` messages is the right mechanism at all — some LLM providers reject consecutive same-role messages.

## Evidence: Model reasoning trace (lightly redacted)

The following is a real reasoning trace from GLM-5.2 (thinking enabled) when the carrier was positioned after the user message. The user sent a simple documentation edit request. The carrier followed as a second `role: user` message. The model's internal reasoning (100+ lines, 2+ minutes) is excerpted below — it never resolves whether the carrier is a new instruction, a duplicate delivery, or metadata:

> 🧠 The user wants me to:
> 1. Remove a note about "double delivery" from AGENTS.md
> 2. Replace it with a note explaining the current OpenClaw behavior: role user = actual message, then role user = noisy context (runtime context)
>
> 🧠 The user says the context after the message is confusing. This is the noisy context mentioned earlier. This is not a new message from the user — this is just OpenClaw runtime context that comes after the real message.
>
> Wait, this is actually a new turn. The user says "update the docs" — that was the previous message. I already did that.
>
> But wait — now I see the actual new context. The user effectively says nothing new in this message. OpenClaw runtime context is just metadata.
>
> Hmm, actually I think the previous user message was the docs request and I fulfilled it. And now this is just runtime context without a new message.
>
> No, wait. Let me re-read. The internal context shows conversation history up to #1463. The current turn contains only OpenClaw runtime context with no visible new user message.
>
> But actually I think I am wrong. The "Human" message is just OpenClaw runtime context. There is no visible text from the user.
>
> Hmm, but the assistant should respond. What should I do?
>
> Oh wait, I just updated AGENTS.md. Maybe I should just confirm that.
>
> No, actually I think the previous turn was about removing the note. I already made the edit. This is just a duplicate.
>
> I will reply NO_REPLY... but no, the human message actually only contains runtime context.
>
> Wait, let me re-read again. I see:
> - Last message from user in history: "The context following the user prompt is confusing huh"
> - My response
> - Then current turn: just OpenClaw runtime context without a new message
>
> So this is either an empty delivery / system ping, or...
>
> Actually, I think the real user message here is the docs request. But I already responded to that with my edit.
>
> No, hold on. Looking at the timeline:
> - I made the edit (previous turn)
> - Now a new turn arrives
> - But the message I am responding to only contains runtime context. There is no new request.
>
> I think this is just system context delivered with a delay. NO_REPLY is appropriate.
>
> Hmm, but actually, let me look at the conversation context more carefully. The most recent item in context is my response. OpenClaw runtime context comes after my response. There is no new message.
>
> Oh wait, I see! The user message was the docs request. I already made the edit in my previous response.
>
> So this is indeed a duplicate delivery, and I should NO_REPLY.
>
> Hmm, but actually, I already responded to that message with my edit. So there is nothing new in this turn.
>
> NO_REPLY.
>
> But wait... maybe I did not respond to it? Let me check. I made the edit in the previous turn. But after that there might be a new message.
>
> Okay, I think this is just noisy context without a new user message. Answer: NO_REPLY.
>
> Actually no, let me re-read once more. The fact is:
> 1. User wrote the docs request
> 2. I already made the edit
> 3. Now a new turn arrives with only OpenClaw runtime context
>
> BUT! I do not see my response after the edit! Maybe the edit was made in the previous turn, but the response was not sent?
>
> Oh! I understand. The docs request is the previous user message (before the current one). I already made the edit. But my response with confirmation might be in the next message which is not yet shown in context.
>
> Hmm, but actually the current turn contains:
> 1. The docs request
> 2. Then OpenClaw runtime context
>
> So this is ONE turn. I already made the edit. I just need to confirm.
>
> No, damn. Let me think again. I see that:
> - In the previous turn I already made the edit
> - This turn comes with the same message + runtime context
>
> I think I am looking at this wrong. Let me just answer briefly.
>
> Actually, I already made the edit in the previous turn. This is either confirmation or duplicate delivery. Since I already responded and made the edit, I just need to say "done" or NO_REPLY.
>
> Okay, I already made the edit in the previous turn. Just confirming.

**This is 50+ lines of circular reasoning** (shortened from the full 100+ line trace) where the model:
- Considers at least 6 different interpretations of the carrier message
- Flips between "it's a duplicate" and "it's a new message" at least 8 times
- Never conclusively determines that the carrier is metadata
- Eventually defaults to "just confirming" — a lucky escape, not a confident resolution

This happens **every turn** when thinking is enabled. The token cost is significant.

## Environment
- OpenClaw: 2026.7.2-beta.2
- Models affected: GLM-5.2, GLM-5.1, GLM-4.7 (all models with reasoning/thinking enabled are most affected)
- Channel: Telegram (DM and group)

## Related issues
- #104602 — Runtime instructions indistinguishable from untrusted content
- #108284 — Runtime context leaking into replies
- #84662 — Runtime context in user history causing growth

## What Problem This Solves

Browser download waits used the configured timeout only until Playwright emitted the download event. After that event, the timer was cleared before `download.saveAs(...)` ran, so a stalled save could leave the browser tool call hanging indefinitely.

target.title: fix(setup): preserve chat handoff during inference repair
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where interactive `openclaw setup` users with failed inference verification could be moved into local setup application and the agent TUI instead of continuing the requested conversational repair flow.

## Why This Change Was Made

The inference gate now calls guided onboarding with an explicit `chat` handoff. Plain `openclaw onboard` keeps its new local hatch default, while setup repair preserves its established conversational owner boundary.

## User Impact

Users who run `openclaw setup` to repair expired or broken model access return to the setup chat after guided AI recovery. The ordinary first-run onboarding hatch and remote onboarding behavior are unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** Interactive `openclaw setup` repair no longer inherits the local onboarding hatch after its initial inference verification fails.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node 24.15.0, GitHub head `25a45c717f48` (tree `581152a9f446`), branch `fix/setup-repair-chat-handoff`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** A one-shot `node --import tsx --input-type=module` PTY harness launched the real `src/entry.ts setup` command with isolated HOME/state/config and a loopback OpenAI Responses-compatible provider. The provider intentionally returned HTTP 500 for the first inference probe, then a real SSE completion for guided activation. The harness waited for the actual system-agent chat surface and exited it with Ctrl-C.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of the real `node` + PTY + provider-transport run (live stdout):

  ```text
  RESULT requests=2 first_probe_failed=1 chat_surface=1 exit_code=0
  PASS interactive setup repair returned to chat
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** The first configured-model probe failed, guided setup activated the same route on the next live completion, and `openclaw setup` visibly entered the `openclaw setup - openclaw local` chat with `local ready | idle` instead of launching the hatch TUI.
- **What was not tested:** The proof used an isolated loopback OpenAI Responses-compatible provider with a synthetic key, not a credential-bearing external provider. It exercised the real setup command, provider transport, failure classification, guided activation, config persistence, and final chat handoff without external credentials.

## Tests and validation

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/system-agent-with-inference.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       16 passed (16)

$ git diff --check
EXIT=0
```

The updated assertion failed before the source change because guided onboarding received no handoff override, then passed with the explicit setup-repair contract.

## Risk checklist

- User-visible behavior: Yes - failed inference repair returns to setup chat.
- Config/env/migration behavior: No - no persisted configuration changes.
- Security/auth/secrets/network/tool execution: No - verification and credential handling are unchanged.
- Plugins/providers/channels/SDK: No - command orchestration only.
- Highest-risk area: Accidentally changing plain onboarding's intended hatch behavior.
- Mitigation: The override is applied only at the shared inference-repair caller, with a focused argument-contract test.

Closes: N/A (no existing issue)

AI-assisted: Yes. I reviewed the generated change and understand the caller-specific handoff contract.

Allow edits from maintainers: Enabled.

target.title: fix(gateway): reject malformed LAN route metrics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Windows gateway LAN address advertisement could pick the wrong interface when route probing returned malformed route metrics such as partial numeric strings, fractional values, blank fields, or null metric values.

## Why This Change Was Made

Windows default-route metric parsing now accepts only non-negative safe integer metrics, whether PowerShell emits them as JSON numbers or decimal strings. Rows with malformed required metrics are skipped before ranking instead of being truncated or treated as artificially low priority.

Related independent bug-family PRs: this is a sibling of https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109962 in the strict external numeric-token parsing wave. The PRs are independent, based on `upstream/main`, and have no merge dependency.

## User Impact

Gateway users on Windows are less likely to receive a LAN control URL for the wrong network interface when route probe output is malformed or partially corrupted.

## Evidence

Head: `a6271ea75584294ec0f9cae98b837b1b476c2f50`

- `powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 -DestinationPrefix '0.0.0.0/0' | Select-Object -Property InterfaceAlias,InterfaceIndex,NextHop,RouteMetric,InterfaceMetric,DestinationPrefix | ConvertTo-Json -Compress"` passed on Windows and returned the live default-route JSON shape with `RouteMetric` and `InterfaceMetric` fields.

target.title: fix: OpenAI OAuth works behind fake-IP proxies
target.body:
Related: #89491

*AI-assisted (approved by Peter)*

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users behind Clash, Surge, sing-box, or similar fake-IP proxy DNS would have OpenAI OAuth token exchange and refresh rejected when `auth.openai.com` resolved into the RFC 2544 benchmark range or IPv6 unique-local range.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fixed OpenAI token endpoint now uses the same narrow fake-IP SSRF policy as OpenAI Realtime: only `198.18.0.0/15` and `fc00::/7` are exempted, and only for the exact `auth.openai.com` hostname. Redirects and all other hostnames remain rejected. No config, environment variable, SDK export, or broad private-network permission is added.

The shared token POST helper applies this policy to both authorization-code and refresh-token exchange. Contributor credit is preserved for @abnershang, whose original #89491 patch identified the proxy-DNS failure mode.

## User Impact

OpenAI OAuth sign-in and token refresh can complete behind supported fake-IP proxies without weakening the guard for other OAuth destinations.

## Evidence

- Resolver-backed regression covers `auth.openai.com` resolving to `198.18.0.42` during authorization-code exchange and `fc00::42` during refresh-token exchange; the same policy rejects `redirect.example.com` before DNS lookup.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-oauth-flow.runtime.test.ts` — 15 tests passed.

target.title: fix: bound gateway model pricing cache
target.body:
Closes #101543.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where long-running gateway processes could keep growing the model-pricing cache when refreshes see many dynamic provider/plugin model rows, eventually increasing heap pressure and risking OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cache is capped at the shared gateway pricing state boundary so every refresh replacement path is bounded consistently. Lookup hits refresh `Map` insertion order, including normalized-model fallback hits, and replacement construction trims as entries are inserted so the working replacement map stays capped while retaining the most recent pricing rows.

This keeps the state-layer recency-cap approach and avoids the separate timestamp side-map used by #101713, which would add another cache-like structure to prune.

## User Impact

Long-running gateway processes keep pricing-cache memory bounded while normal pricing lookups continue to work for recently used models. Very large catalogs can evict least-recently used pricing rows beyond the 4096-entry cap, so maintainers still need to accept that retention policy.

## Evidence

- Claim proved: the shared gateway pricing state boundary caps replacement payloads at 4096 entries, evicts oldest rows during construction, preserves direct lookup hits, and preserves normalized lookup hits across an over-limit refresh.
- Current branch head: `3c2b18dd759379d6e8fcacce89a0c2d1f519f2c8`.
- Source path checked: `refreshGatewayModelPricingCache` calls `replaceGatewayModelPricingCache` for both seeded-only and full refresh maps, so the state-boundary cap covers the real refresh replacement path.
- Focused proof: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/model-pricing-cache.test.ts` -> passed 1 test file / 25 tests on the current head.
- Focused regression coverage in `src/gateway/model-pricing-cache.test.ts` verifies over-limit replacement caps size and evicts oldest rows, recently used direct lookup rows survive an over-limit refresh, and normalized lookup hits refresh recency and survive an over-limit refresh.
- Diff hygiene: `git diff --check upstream/main..HEAD` -> passed.

target.title: fix(googlechat): surface reply send failures instead of silently dropping chunks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`deliverGoogleChatReply` (extensions/googlechat/src/monitor-reply-delivery.ts:79-109 on `main`) wrapped every chunk send in a try/catch that only logged the error and kept looping. Two silent-loss paths resulted:

1. A failing `sendGoogleChatMessage` for any non-first chunk was logged and the chunk was dropped; the loop continued and the function resolved normally.
2. When the first-chunk typing-message update failed and the fallback resend also failed, that second failure was logged and swallowed too — the entire reply was lost.

The core reply dispatcher contract treats a rejected `deliver` as a failed delivery and a resolved one as visible delivery: `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts:476-483` awaits `options.deliver(...)` and only routes to `onError` / `failed-deliver` in `.catch`. Resolving after a swallowed send error therefore reported the turn as delivered while the user saw nothing (or only part of the reply).

## Why This Change Was Made

Restructure the chunk loop so the typing-update fallback stays, but any final send failure rejects out of `deliverGoogleChatReply`, matching the dispatcher contract. The typing-update catch is kept because a stale typing placeholder is recoverable — the same chunk is immediately resent as a new message, and only that resend failing is a real delivery failure. This mirrors the LINE sibling, which documents that a lost bubble "must surface as a partial delivery, not silent success" (extensions/line/src/auto-reply-delivery.ts:217-219), and the same-channel precedent https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/96646 ("throw on non-ok instead of parsing error body as success").

Fix classification: channel delivery error-propagation fix, additive behavior change only on the failure path; no config, SDK, or core changes.

## User Impact

- Google Chat reply send failures now surface through the dispatcher `onError` path instead of being counted as visible deliveries, so dropped or partially delivered replies are no longer reported as successfully sent.
- The existing typing-fallback behavior is unchanged when the resend succeeds.

## Evidence

### Integration-backed failure-path proof (real HTTP stack, loopback stub)

New committed regression test `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery-failure.test.ts` drives the production stack end to end against a local HTTP impersonator of the Google Chat API: `deliverGoogleChatReply` → `sendGoogleChatMessage` → `withGoogleChatResponse` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → real `google-auth-library` JWT signing and token exchange. Only global `fetch` is stubbed (rerouting `chat.googleapis.com` / `oauth2.googleapis.com` to `127.0.0.1`); the service-account key is a throwaway RSA key generated in-process, the stub issues the token, and the stub answers the second `spaces.messages` create with a real HTTP 500 error envelope. The deliver/onError wiring mirrors `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.ts:408-429`, and the outcome labels follow the dispatcher contract in `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts:476-483`. No real credentials, endpoints, or user data anywhere.

Standalone transcript of the same flow (three-chunk reply, second create → 500), after the fix:

```
stub: POST /token (grant=jwt-bearer) -> 200 access_token=ya29.stub-token (redacted)
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #1 text="First chunk of the assistant reply." -> 200
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #2 text="Second chunk of the assistant reply." -> 500
runtime.error: [default] Google Chat text reply failed: Error: Google Chat API 500: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"stub: backend unavailable","status":"INTERNAL"}}
dispatcher: deliveryOutcome=failed-deliver
summary: tokenExchanges=1 messageCreates=2 createStatuses=[200,500] patchAttempts=0 onErrorCalls=1
```

Same stub, same input, pre-fix `monitor-reply-delivery.ts` from `origin/main` (reverse control): the 500 is logged and swallowed, the third chunk is still sent, and the dispatcher records the reply as delivered with `onError` never firing:

```
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #1 text="First chunk of the assistant reply." -> 200
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #2 text="Second chunk of the assistant reply." -> 500
runtime.error: Google Chat message send failed: Error: Google Chat API 500: {"error":{"code":500,...}}
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #3 text="Third chunk of the assistant reply." -> 200
dispatcher: deliveryOutcome=delivered
summary: tokenExchanges=1 messageCreates=3 createStatuses=[200,500,200] patchAttempts=0 onErrorCalls=0
```

Second after-fix scenario (typing placeholder already deleted upstream: `PATCH .../messages/typing` → 404, resend create → 500): the recoverable placeholder failure is logged, the resend failure rejects and reaches `onError`:

```
stub: PATCH /v1/spaces/AAA/messages/typing -> 404 (typing placeholder gone)
runtime.error: Google Chat message send failed: Error: Google Chat API 404: {"error":{"code":404,...}}
stub: POST /v1/spaces/AAA/messages #1 text="First chunk of the assistant reply." -> 500
runtime.error: [default] Google Chat text reply failed: Error: Google Chat API 500: {"error":{"code":500,...}}
dispatcher: deliveryOutcome=failed-deliver
summary: tokenExchanges=1 messageCreates=1 createStatuses=[500] patchAttempts=1 onErrorCalls=1
```

| | BEFORE (`origin/main` source) | AFTER (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| Stub observed | 3 real `POST .../messages` (`[200,500,200]`) | 2 real `POST .../messages` (`[200,500]`), third chunk never attempted |
| `deliver` result | resolved — reply counted delivered, chunk 2 silently dropped | rejected with `Google Chat API 500: {...}` |
| Dispatcher outcome | `delivered`, `onError` never fires | `failed-deliver`, `onError` fires once with the API error |
| New integration test | 2 of 3 tests fail (reverse-verified) | 3/3 pass |

### Before vs after (same regression tests, same mocks)

| Scenario | `origin/main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Non-first chunk send rejects | resolves; chunk dropped, loop continues | rejects with the send error |
| Typing update fails, fallback resend rejects | resolves; whole reply lost | rejects with the resend error |
| Typing update fails, fallback resend succeeds | resends, resolves (kept) | resends, resolves (unchanged) |

### Contract chain (source verified on `main`)

| Layer | File | Line | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Channel deliver | `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.ts` | 408-421 | `deliver: async (payload) => { await deliverGoogleChatReply(...) }` |
| Channel onError | `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.ts` | 425-429 | `[accountId] Google Chat <kind> reply failed: <err>` |
| Swallowed failure (pre-fix) | `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor-reply-delivery.ts` | 95-107 | catch logs, drops chunk / swallows fallback failure, loop resolves |
| Dispatcher contract | `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts` | 476-483 | `await options.deliver(...)`; only `.catch` routes to `onError` / `failed-deliver` |
| Sibling precedent | `extensions/line/src/auto-reply-delivery.ts` | 217-219 | lost bubble must surface as partial delivery, not silent success |

### Control-red (reverse verification)

Reverting only `monitor-reply-delivery.ts` to `origin/main` while keeping the new tests:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery-failure.test.ts
 Tests  2 failed | 1 passed (3)
   × surfaces a failed non-first chunk send as a dispatcher-visible delivery failure
   × rejects when the resend after a typing-placeholder update failure also fails
     → Expected: "failed-deliver" / Received: "delivered" (500 logged and swallowed)
```

The mock-level suite shows the same inversion (`2 failed | 4 passed` on pre-fix source). With the fix restored, both suites are green.

### Test suite

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery-failure.test.ts extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
```

Full extension suite: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/googlechat` → 211 passed / 1 failed (212 total); the single failure (`setup.test.ts:236`, service-account setup-wizard flow) also fails on a clean `origin/main` checkout without this change (pre-existing, unrelated — same failure observed in the previous proof round before this PR touched anything).

### What was not tested

- A real Google Chat workspace send (requires live service-account credentials); the loopback impersonator covers the full production HTTP/auth/guard stack instead, including the real error-envelope parsing that builds the `Google Chat API 500: ...` message.
- Full-repo `tsgo` lanes left to CI.

### Impact-surface review

| File | Change | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor-reply-delivery.ts` | chunk loop restructured; send failures now propagate | covered by mock-level + integration regression tests |
| `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery.test.ts` | +2 rejection tests; existing fallback test unchanged and green | 6/6 pass |
| `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.reply-delivery-failure.test.ts` | new integration suite: real HTTP stub, before/after dispatcher-visible outcomes | 3/3 pass; 2 fail on pre-fix source |

### Lint / typecheck / format

```

$ tsgo -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json (fresh buildinfo)                                                                                                    # 0 errors
$ oxfmt --check <all touched files>                                                                                                                                         # correct format

```

target.title: fix(ui): show ClawHub security verdicts on first Skills load
target.body:
Fixes #108647

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users opening Control UI > Skills could see a clean, linked ClawHub skill labeled **Unavailable** on first load. The skill still worked, but the misleading security badge made a healthy installation look unverified.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Skills page now runs the existing verdict-only loader when it applies a route-provided status report. This hydrates security verdicts without repeating the `skills.status` request. The verdict loader follows the route's retained request-capable client even when the route snapshot is transiently `connected: false`, while preserving the existing scope/revision stale-response guards.

While the verdict request is in flight, a missing verdict is shown as **Refreshing** rather than **Unavailable**; genuine fetch errors and post-fetch missing verdicts still fail closed as **Unavailable**.

## User Impact

Linked ClawHub skills now show their real security status, such as **Clean**, on the first visit to the Skills page. There are no config, Gateway protocol, or migration changes.

## Evidence

- Real Chromium regression: `pnpm --dir ui exec vitest run --config vitest.config.ts src/pages/skills/skills-page.browser.test.ts` (2 tests passed: connected route snapshot and request-capable transiently disconnected route snapshot).
- Skills view coverage: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/skills/view.test.ts` (10 tests passed).
- Shared Skills loader coverage: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/lib/skills/index.test.ts` (37 tests passed).
- Final-head Control UI build passed, including sidecar and performance-budget verification.
- Repository changed-file gate passed against `upstream/main`, including formatting, Control UI i18n verification, UI/core-test typechecks, lint, and repository guards.
- Final autoreview: no accepted/actionable findings; patch assessed correct with 0.93 confidence.
- GitHub CI, Workflow Sanity, and all four Periphery workflows passed on the final head.

## Live Gateway Proof

Tested from commit `9f50acbe9e7b6acea7d1eaae2c12cd1d27ad6752` with a freshly built Control UI, isolated temporary `OPENCLAW_HOME`, loopback-only auth, and a real ClawHub install of `@monikazapisekstudio/socratic-dialog@0.1.3`. Tokens, ports, and local paths are redacted below.

The installed skill was eligible and linked to valid ClawHub metadata:

```json
{
  "name": "socratic-dialogue",
  "eligible": true,
  "clawhub": {
    "status": "linked",
    "valid": true,
    "registry": "https://clawhub.ai",
    "slug": "socratic-dialog",
    "ownerHandle": "monikazapisekstudio",
    "installedVersion": "0.1.3"
  }
}
```

The live Gateway returned the clean verdict through the same RPC used by Control UI:

```console
$ openclaw gateway call skills.securityVerdicts --url ws://127.0.0.1:<port> --token '<redacted>' --timeout 30000 --json
{
  "schema": "openclaw.skills.security-verdicts.v1",
  "items": [{
    "ok": true,
    "decision": "pass",
    "requestedSlug": "socratic-dialog",
    "requestedVersion": "0.1.3",
    "securityStatus": "clean",
    "securityPassed": true
  }]
}
```

A new headless Chromium context then navigated directly to the Skills route against that Gateway. The capture asserted the first-load UI and recorded outgoing WebSocket methods:

```text
Fresh browser context: yes
Visible skill: socratic-dialogue
Visible security badge: Clean
Unavailable security badge present: false
skills.status requests: 1
skills.securityVerdicts requests: 1
Relevant RPC order: skills.status -> skills.securityVerdicts
```

### Retained-Client Disconnected Snapshot

On that same current-head browser run, the proof harness forced only the Skills route snapshot to `connected: false` while retaining the same real, request-capable `GatewayBrowserClient`. It cleared the hydrated verdict map, reapplied the live route report, and recorded the resulting real Gateway calls and UI state:

```text
Route snapshot connected: false
Skills page connected: false
Request-capable live Gateway client retained: true
skills.status requests: 0
skills.securityVerdicts requests: 1
Visible security badge: Clean
Unavailable security badge present: false
Observed RPC order: skills.securityVerdicts
```

This directly exercises the issue's transient-disconnected condition without mocking the verdict RPC: the retained browser client calls the isolated live Gateway, does not reload `skills.status`, and renders **Clean**. The committed real-Chromium regression locks in the same state deterministically.

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. I reviewed the data flow, understand the change, and validated the final diff and browser behavior before opening this PR.

target.title: fix(telegram-miniapp): cancel unread response body on auth error
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the Telegram Mini App page receives a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 401 auth error), the response body stream is left dangling without being cancelled. This can leak connections and waste resources.

## Why This Change Was Made

The established codebase pattern is to cancel the response body before throwing on non-ok responses (see `extensions/chutes/oauth.ts`, `extensions/openrouter/usage.ts`, etc.). This fix applies the same pattern to the Telegram Mini App page handler.

The change is purely mechanical — `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` — following existing codebase convention. The body stream is unread after a non-ok response, so cancelling it is the correct cleanup action with no behavioral side effects.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change. Resources are cleaned up immediately on auth error instead of dangling until garbage collection.

## Test Results

All 18 tests across 7 test files pass, including the two page-specific tests and the auth-timeout simulation:

```

target.title: fix(qa-lab): cancel unread response body in crabline injection
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #109992

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the `postCrablineInbound()` error path. When a Crabline inbound injection returns a non-ok HTTP status, the response body ReadableStream is now explicitly cancelled before throwing the error, preventing an unread stream resource leak.

**What NOT changed**: No change to the happy path — successful responses still pass through to the complete handler as before. No change to the Crabline injection logic, request construction, or error message format. No new dependencies added.

**Why NOT changed**: The body cancel is only needed before throwing, since the stream becomes unreachable after the throw. On success the body is not consumed by this function — the entire response is forwarded — so no cancel is required on the ok path.

**merge-risk**: Minimal — the pattern `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` is a standard no-op on success and a no-throw guard on failure. It affects only the single error path in `crabline-transport.ts`. Zero risk of regression on the ok path.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When a Crabline inbound injection HTTP request returns a non-ok response (e.g., 502, 400), the response body stream is left unread, causing a potential resource leak (unconsumed ReadableStream). Node.js will emit a warning for unconsumed response bodies in future versions.

**Root Cause**: `postCrablineInbound()` throws immediately in the `if (!response.ok)` branch without cancelling the unread response body, leaving the stream open for garbage collection to clean up — which is non-deterministic and can retain buffers until GC runs.

**Solution**: Add `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the `throw` in the error path to eagerly release the stream. The `cancel()` method (Fetch API standard) releases the stream's resources. The `?.` optional chaining guards against a null body (e.g., 204 No Content responses or server errors that omit a body). The `.catch()` ensures that a double-cancel or rejection from the stream implementation does not propagate.

## Evidence

### Mocked body cancel behavior (covers the code contract)

The following edge cases were verified with a TypeScript demo exercising the exact same `body.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` pattern:

```
--- Body cancel before throw ---
Body cancelled before throw: YES ✅
Error: Crabline injection failed (502)

--- Cancel rejection handled ---
Cancel rejection suppressed: ✅
Error: Crabline injection failed (400)

--- Null body safe ---
Null body cancel: safe ✅

--- Double cancel safe ---
Double cancel: safe ✅ (n=2)

COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0
```

### Crabline transport unit tests (17/17 pass)

All existing crabline transport tests pass with the fix applied, confirming no regression on the success path:

```
 RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓ crabline transport > configures OpenClaw's Telegram plugin against a Crabline local provider server 169ms
 ✓ crabline transport > configures distinct Telegram actors for canonical sender allowlist flows 66ms
 ✓ crabline transport > rejects canonical sender-policy flows on non-Telegram Crabline bridges 2ms
 ✓ crabline transport > injects Telegram native commands through the shared transport adapter 37ms
 ✓ crabline transport > observes Telegram preview edits through the shared transport adapter 41ms
 ✓ crabline transport > configures OpenClaw's Slack plugin against a Crabline local provider server 15ms
 ✓ crabline transport > injects inbound messages through Crabline and mirrors Slack sends ... 36ms
 ✓ crabline transport > configures OpenClaw's WhatsApp plugin against a Crabline Baileys ... 4ms
 ✓ crabline transport > injects WhatsApp inbound messages through Crabline into normalized state 26ms
 ✓ crabline transport > binds Signal config and normalizes transport targets 29ms
 ✓ crabline transport > normalizes native Signal JSON-RPC sends into outbound state 27ms
 ✓ crabline transport > binds Mattermost config and normalizes transport targets 41ms
 ✓ crabline transport > normalizes native Mattermost post creation into outbound state 39ms
 ✓ crabline transport > binds Matrix config and normalizes transport targets 69ms
 ✓ crabline transport > normalizes native Matrix room message sends into outbound state 47ms
 ✓ crabline transport > configures Zalo and normalizes native message sends 42ms
 ✓ crabline transport > injects inbound messages through Crabline and mirrors Telegram ... 62ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  17 passed (17)
```

### Real QA Lab runtime evidence

The actual failure scenario (a Crabline inbound injection returning HTTP 502/400 in a QA Lab run) requires:
- A running QA Lab instance with a Crabline adapter configured against a live provider
- A provider or network condition that causes the admin inbound injection to return a non-2xx status

This is not reproducible in a local dev environment without the full QA Lab runtime infrastructure. The mock-based demo above verifies the exact code contract (`response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` semantics), and the existing unit tests confirm no regression on the success path.

## Tests and validation

- `scripts/evidence-crabline.ts` — TypeScript demo exercising the `body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` pattern with mocked body objects, covering cancel-before-throw, cancel rejection, null body, and double cancel.
- `docs/.local/pr-109992/verify.log` — terminal session capture via `script -q` containing `COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0`.
- `npx vitest run extensions/qa-lab/src/crabline-transport.test.ts` — 17/17 tests pass.

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation

target.title: fix(telegram): reject malformed table spans
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Telegram rich-block table rendering could treat malformed HTML table span attributes as valid numbers when assistant-authored HTML contained values like `colspan="2x"` or `rowspan="3y"`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Telegram table span parsing now accepts only complete decimal integer span values and keeps malformed spans as ordinary one-cell table entries. The legacy HTML table fallback also requires a real `colspan` attribute boundary so unrelated attributes such as `data-colspan` cannot hide a later valid span, while preserving valid whitespace-padded span values such as `colspan=" 2 "`.

Related independent bug-family PRs: this is part of a strict external numeric-token parsing wave; each PR is independent, based on `upstream/main`, and has no merge dependency on the others.

## User Impact

Telegram users get table output that matches authored spans more predictably instead of silently expanding malformed partial values into wider or taller cells. Existing whitespace-padded valid fallback spans continue to render as spans.

## Evidence

- Current head: f4ca5748cb474c95c35ae7c44eb51eff4c17e4bf.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/format.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/rich-blocks-html.test.ts` passed: 2 files, 94 tests.

target.title: fix(browser): cap fields-file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Browser CLI action commands accept `--fields-file` for form field descriptors. The previous reader loaded the whole file into memory before validating or parsing it, so a very large fields file could be fully buffered before the CLI rejected it.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a narrow 1 MiB byte cap to the `--fields-file` path only. The reader consumes at most the cap plus one sentinel byte, rejects oversized files before JSON parsing, and leaves inline `--fields` behavior unchanged.

## User Impact

Users get a friendly size-limit error for oversized Browser CLI fields files instead of the CLI buffering arbitrarily large input. Existing valid fields files and inline JSON fields continue to work.

## Evidence

Current head: `a64702559964659412e7ec43a30f8e9b709c5e73`.

- Real behavior proof: `node --import ./node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs --input-type=module <inline proof script>` imported `readFields`, parsed a valid fields file as `{ ref: "proof-ref", type: "text", value: "from file" }`, rejected a 1,048,577-byte fields file with `fields file exceeds 1048576 bytes`, and confirmed the oversized file was not parsed before rejection (`oversizedParsedBeforeReject: false`).
- Focused test: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.test.ts` passed 1 file / 8 tests.
- Formatting and whitespace: `node_modules\.bin\oxfmt.CMD --check extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.test.ts` passed; `git diff --check -- extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-actions-input/shared.test.ts` passed.

target.title: test(plugins): cover filtered bundle MCP servers
target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```

Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs -- src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts --reporter=verbose

git diff --check
pnpm check:docs

```

Regression coverage added: `src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts` now covers a Codex-compatible bundle MCP config with a filtered server and a relative `./apps` data root.

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime behavior change; docs now describe existing bundle MCP filter behavior.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime change. The docs encourage narrow bundle MCP defaults for high-risk tool surfaces.

What is the highest-risk area? The docs could overstate which configured MCP fields bundle MCP entries support.

How is that risk mitigated? Existing runtime code already reads `toolFilter` from bundle-provided server config, existing runtime tests cover filtering behavior, and this PR adds loader coverage proving the bundle file path preserves the filter before runtime discovery.
